content_list.content_text: Although American independent cinema enjoyed one of its great moments in the 1980s and 1990s, it was by no means a phenomenon confined to that period. True independent cinema - produced outside the major studios - is nothing new in the United States. Small studios and lone filmmakers have been making their own productions since the earliest days of cinema.

content_list.content_text: Rather than being defined simply by production and distribution criteria, indie cinema is, at least in theory, cinema with ideas of its own, resistant to the norms of the mainstream and loosely tied to the counterculture. American independent films are seen as the creations of filmmakers with distinctive points of view, who usually produce and retain the rights to their work. This tradition includes names as varied as Andy Warhol (1929-1989), Robert Altman (1925-2006), John Cassavetes (1929-1987), and George A. Romero (b. 1940).

content_list.content_text: American independent film flourished as a visible culture in the 1980s. Key figures were the versatile John Sayles (b. 1950), making dramas against authoritarianism such as Matewan (1987), and Jim Jarmusch (b. 1953), whose laconic, hip style has its roots in the zero-budget New York scene of the late 1970s.

Joel Coen (b. 1954) and Ethan Coen (b. 1957) first made their mark in 1984 with the black comedy Blood Simple (1984). A major turning point came in 1986, when Spike Lee (b. 1957) emerged with the sex comedy She's Gotta Have It (1986). His stylistic inventiveness, political provocation and hard-nosed entrepreneurship paved the way for a new wave of African American directors, such as John Singleton (b. 1968), Matty Rich (b. 1971) and the twins Albert Hughes and Allen Hughes (b. 1972), as well as for more experimental voices such as Julie Dash (b. 1952).

information.contentText: The film, whose title refers to the pulp magazines popular during the mid-20th century and known for their graphic violence, is famous for its rich, eclectic dialogue, ironic mix of humor and violence, nonlinear narrative, and a host of allusions to other films and references to pop culture.

content_list.title: No Country for Old Men — Don't Underestimate the Audience
content_list.description: No Country For Old Men is a film that challenges its audience in the best possible way. It never condescends and refuses to spell things out - instead, it compels us to connect the dots and take part in the storytelling. This video examines some of the ways it achieves this.

movie.overview: Llewelyn Moss stumbles upon dead bodies, $2 million and a hoard of heroin in a Texas desert, but methodical killer Anton Chigurh comes looking for it, with local sheriff Ed Tom Bell hot on his trail. The roles of prey and predator blur as the violent pursuit of money and justice collide.
movie.title: No Country for Old Men

content_list.content_text: Many of these pioneers have sustained long careers of remarkable diversity. Sayles still makes critically acclaimed films, such as the unconventional Western Lone Star (1996) and the adoption drama Casa de los Babys (2003). Jarmusch continues to break boundaries with films such as the Western Dead Man (1995) and the series of vignettes about celebrities Coffee and Cigarettes (2003).

content_list.title: Tarantino's Definitive Signature
content_list.description:
From whatever angle one chooses to analyze Pulp Fiction, the conclusion is inescapable that it was not only one of the most important films of the '90s but also a major influence on an entire generation, a cinematic watershed, so to speak. The unmistakable filmmaking style that Quentin Tarantino had so firmly established with his Reservoir Dogs just two years earlier, blending varied techniques into a unique and original result, reached a kind of early climax with Pulp Fiction, since renowned filmmakers usually have a significant growth curve, which can last decades, before reaching their peak. And I would not even dare to state categorically, after all these years, that Tarantino's second feature really is his high point, because I honestly could no longer say; however, without a shadow of a doubt, this is the film that threw the doors wide open for the director and that also seeped most deeply, immediately, and indelibly into pop culture, with a veritable avalanche of iconic dialogue, unforgettable songs, and breathtaking sequences.

But what makes Pulp Fiction Pulp Fiction? That is a question that can have a myriad of answers, all of them valid. In my view, however, the work's great highlight is the way Tarantino, who wrote the screenplay based on stories created by himself and Roger Avary (b. 1965), tells three largely independent stories - four, if we count the one about the couple trying to steal some money, which opens and closes the film - inspired by the kind of literature the title openly announces, in a complex nonlinear narrative structure, each with its own beginning, middle, and end, but all in dialogue with one another within the overall theme of the criminal underworld in and around Los Angeles.

It is easy to spot films that were influenced by Pulp, such as Memento and City of God. The transformation - or, perhaps, appropriation - of nonlinear narrative as something of his own is, I would say, one of Tarantino's most misunderstood traits. The director is accused of being a copycat, a plagiarist, and every synonym for it, as if no other director did the same, or as if Tarantino himself had not stated that he uses references to works he likes to a greater or lesser degree. But what the director knows how to do is turn everything he "copies or borrows" into something easily identifiable as his own. We know we are watching a Tarantino film even if we come to it halfway through. The same can be said of directors such as Woody Allen and Steven Spielberg. Whether that is a good or bad thing is not for us to judge here. What is clear is that Tarantino knows how to turn what is seemingly commonplace into his signature, and that is what he did with nonlinear narrative in Pulp Fiction: he transformed the basics into a structure that unfolds into several parallel and sometimes tangential stories which, in the end, make plain the director's command of the camera and of editing, not to mention the ever-present and always perfect soundtrack, another cinematic watershed, by the way.

Each of the narrative threads that populate Tarantino's episodic film is riddled with dialogue that works as an expansion of what we saw in his first film. While his first film had dialogue confined to a single circle of people made up of white gangsters or bank robbers, in Pulp Fiction we see a mix of different characters in a pair dynamic (or nearly so): the couple of amateur robbers who open and close the film (Tim Roth and Amanda Plummer); the hitman duo Vincent Vega (John Travolta, revived by Tarantino) and Jules Winnfield (Samuel L. Jackson, revealed to the world here) on a mission; crime boss Marsellus Wallace (Ving Rhames) and Butch (Willis), a boxer in the twilight of his career, running into the rapists Zed (Peter Greene) and Maynard (Duane Whitaker); Vincent Vega and Mia Wallace (Uma Thurman) grappling with a heroin overdose and with drug dealer Lance (Eric Stoltz) and his wife Jody (Rosanna Arquette); and Vincent, Jules, Jimmie (Tarantino himself), and "problem solver" Mr. Wolf (Harvey Keitel) dealing with an unpleasant situation involving blood and bits of brain splattered all over a car.

Each line of dialogue is carefully crafted to fit its character and that character's interaction with the other. There is a bit of everything, plus Tarantino's incredible ability to slip in pop culture references at every turn. The lines about the little differences between Europe and the United States, about Marsellus getting "medieval" on Zed, about the Bible passage Jules quotes before killing, and many others are, if we like, as empty of content as they are full of rhythm; or as full of social criticism as we choose to imagine, without forgetting that several of them are lifted - some word for word - from earlier works, in yet another demonstration of Tarantino's ability to remix what already exists and make it his own.

Pulp Fiction, with all its extreme violence (there are bits of brain in Vince and Jules's hair!), is a feast for the eyes and ears, as well as being educational. After all, where else could you learn that in Amsterdam they serve beer in glasses at the movie theater, or that a foot massage always has a sexual connotation?
content_list.credits: Summary based on the article "Crítica | Pulp Fiction – Tempo de Violência" by Ritter Fan in Plano Crítico.

content_list.content_text: Lee continued to examine relationships in Jungle Fever (1991) and explored documentary with When the Levees Broke: A Requiem in Four Acts (2006). The Coen brothers found fame beyond cinephile circles with Barton Fink (1991) and Fargo (1996). The Coens have since worked in a variety of commercial contexts, but the singularity of their consistent and sometimes perverse vision qualifies them as models of independence. David Lynch (b. 1946) developed his career in a similar way to the Coen brothers, starting out as the quintessential outsider with the frightening oddity of Eraserhead (1977).

content_list.content_text: Launched in 1982, the Sundance Film Festival (as it has been called since 1991) put its seal on an independent film culture that thrived partly as a reaction to the prevailing conservatism of President Ronald Reagan's administration. Sundance launched the careers of many filmmakers, among them Steven Soderbergh (b. 1963), who won the Sundance Audience Award for sex, lies, and videotape (1989). The film drew attention to the new low-budget cinema by earning an Oscar nomination and the Palme d'Or at the Cannes Film Festival.

Since then, as a director and producer, Soderbergh has experimented with every kind of genre on every imaginable kind of budget, both inside and outside the mainstream. Robert Rodriguez (b. 1968) burst onto the scene at Sundance with the action film El Mariachi (1993), originally conceived for the low-cost Spanish-language home video market. After its phenomenal success, Rodriguez opened his own mini-studio, becoming a kind of Roger Corman (b. 1926) with a Latin accent.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from sex, lies, and videotape
information.contentText: With a budget of just $1.2 million, Soderbergh rehearsed for a week and shot the film in a month. He later said it was "the only film I've made where I felt I had all the money and all the time I needed." The film was a hit and became one of the biggest influences on independent cinema in the 1990s.

content_list.title: Wes Anderson Explains How to Write & Direct Movies | The Director's Chair
content_list.description: Do you want to learn the secrets of Wes Anderson's filmmaking style? His unique writing and directing style attracts the biggest movie stars, such as Bill Murray, Ed Norton, and Bruce Willis. He teamed up with Owen Wilson and Luke Wilson for years, and while his writing definitely contributes, what can you learn from Wes Anderson interviews or Wes Anderson quotes? What is so special about Wes Anderson's cinematography or the Wes Anderson aesthetic?

content_list.content_text: Kevin Smith (b. 1970) showed up at Sundance with the raucous Clerks (1994), shot in the convenience store where he worked. An enthusiastic amateur who made it big, Smith remains the quintessential representative of the indie scene.

content_list.content_text: Another important strand was the so-called "New Queer Cinema." An international phenomenon, in the United States its pioneers included Todd Haynes (b. 1961) with Poison (1991) and Gus Van Sant (b. 1952) with Mala Noche (1987). Both directors transcended the label with formally innovative films. Likewise, women found more room to create singular work in the independent sector, among them Allison Anders (b. 1954), with her study of a Hispanic gang in Los Angeles, Mi Vida Loca (1994), and Maggie Greenwald (b. 1955), with the revisionist Western The Ballad of Little Jo (1993).

information.contentText: It is considered the cheapest film in history, costing only US$7,725 to complete, and it became the cheapest film ever acquired for distribution by a major American studio. In 1992, at just 23 years old, Robert Rodriguez showed the world how his creativity could break through the tiny budget he had: he performed every crew role on El Mariachi himself. According to the director, the only reason he didn't act in it as well was that there would have been no one to hold the camera. To shoot scenes with a moving camera, Robert Rodriguez used a broken wheelchair he got from a hospital. Most of the guns seen in the film were actually water pistols. The exception was the ones used by the police officers, which were real and had been lent by the local police station.

content_list.content_text: Independent cinema provided a haven for experimental filmmakers, such as Todd Solondz (b. 1959), with provocative social satires like Happiness (1998); Larry Clark (b. 1943), with his portraits of urban teenagers such as the gutsy Kids (1995); Paul Thomas Anderson (b. 1970), with elegant ensemble pieces like Boogie Nights (1997); and Wes Anderson (b. 1969), with clever works like The Royal Tenenbaums (2001). Vincent Gallo (b. 1961) made his directorial debut with a film about a wrongly accused ex-convict, Buffalo '66 (1998), which won him a following of admirers for its reinterpretation of the genre, its eccentric soundtrack, and its innovative cinematography.

content_list.title: The Cynicism of the Coen Brothers
content_list.description:
One of the specialties of brothers and partners Joel and Ethan Coen is twisting well-established Hollywood genres into delightful, exuberant contemporary forms. The films of this duo, two of the most important filmmakers to emerge in the United States in the 1980s, remain excellent, and the fiendishly clever Fargo ranks among the best. It is a sordid tale that draws gasps of admiration and shock, but also big laughs. On screen are embezzlement, kidnapping, deceptions, misunderstandings, and murder, as well as another constant in the Coens' films: a crime that spins completely out of control.

The Coens' clever ideas yield a peculiar, bizarre tragicomedy that manages to be both hugely entertaining and violently disturbing, through impeccably executed twists that contrast the essential effectiveness and innocence of some characters with the depravity of others. The hapless criminals and their victims are not there to elicit empathy, but to be cruelly manipulated for our amusement. The cold, malevolent spirit that has resurfaced in many of their other films led one critic of their work to call them "artsy annoyances." But that does not diminish their flagrant talent for astonishing, bewildering, and entertaining audiences. Despite its stark look, Fargo is one of the brothers' most tender works, full of signature sequences and running gags that stretch across several scenes, but also with the redemptive comfort of plain decency. McDormand and the Coens' screenplay won two Oscars for breaking the old rules in a one-of-a-kind murder case.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text by Angela Errigo, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

content_list.content_text: The comedy Slacker (1990) by Richard Linklater (b. 1960) embodied an indie aesthetic and also defined a subculture; his subsequent career would include both commercial films and experimental works such as the animated Waking Life (2001). Sofia Coppola (b. 1971), daughter of Francis Ford Coppola (b. 1939), showed that cinema ran in her veins with her brilliant feature debut The Virgin Suicides (2000), and won the Oscar for Best Original Screenplay for Lost in Translation (2003). After the experimental costume drama Marie Antoinette (2006), she revisited some of her themes in the spare Somewhere (2010).

information.contentText: Drawing on a range of influences, including the films The Fire Within and The Magnificent Ambersons, the story deals with themes such as family dysfunction, lost greatness, and redemption, all with an absurd, ironic sense of humor and a pop soundtrack that was later released on two albums.

content_list.title: How the Coen Brothers Direct Comedy & Violence
content_list.description: The Coen brothers are two directors with one vision. Perhaps working as a pair helps them cover such a wide range of subjects, from Looney Tunes-style comedies to dark, fatalistic thrillers. And they seem to operate within these disparate modes with equal skill and control. Few filmmakers have such a definitive style, and we're here to see if we can decode the Coen Brothers' cinematic DNA. Using seven areas of focus, including cinematography, sound design, and editing, we'll work through their filmography to isolate how each piece of the puzzle fits together.

content_list.content_text: Still, the king of the film geeks remains Quentin Tarantino (b. 1963), whose obsessive cinephile energies (first unleashed in the inventive, economical tale of a jewel heist, Reservoir Dogs (1992)) led him to be hailed as cinema's wunderkind, his films packed with pop culture references. Tarantino's reputation has fluctuated, but he remains the main point of reference for fans of indie filmmaking. With Pulp Fiction (1994), he became one of the leading forces of independent cinema in the 1990s and 2000s, following up with films such as Kill Bill: Vol. 1 (2003), Kill Bill: Vol. 2 (2004) and what is probably his masterpiece alongside Pulp Fiction, Inglourious Basterds (2009).

Independent films also had an impact on documentaries, mainly thanks to investigative essays by Michael Moore (b. 1954) such as Roger & Me (1989) and Bowling for Columbine (2002). The impact of Moore's work spurred a new wave of extremely diverse documentaries, from the traditional social realism of Hoop Dreams (1994), by Steve James (b. 1954), to the more idiosyncratic storytelling of Capturing the Friedmans (2003), directed by Andrew Jarecki (b. 1963).

information.contentText: Tarantino originally approached Leonardo DiCaprio to play Hans Landa, before deciding the character should be played by a German actor. The role ultimately went to Austrian actor Christoph Waltz, who, according to Tarantino, "gave me my movie," since he had feared the role was "unplayable."

content_list.content_text: The indie world has been fertile ground for genre fans. The biggest success is The Blair Witch Project (1999), shot on video, a horror mockumentary that heralded a new wave of low-budget chillers. Money, of course, matters. Genre works can suffer from financial constraints.

quote.quote: My movies are my children. I love them all, but at the end of the day, I'll always have a soft spot for Reservoir Dogs. It was my first, the one that changed my life.
quote.author: Quentin Tarantino

content_list.content_text: Dramas thrive even with an almost theatrical scarcity of resources, whereas horror and science fiction are harder to produce when expectations have been fed by years of groundbreaking special effects. Even so, far from the glitter of big budgets, fresh ideas expressed inventively can produce science fiction that works by any measure. Gattaca (1997), Donnie Darko (2001), and A Scanner Darkly (2006) are independent productions reminiscent of the intimate science fiction of Alphaville (1965), by Jean-Luc Godard (b. 1930).

A group of independent production companies came to dominate the circuit, among them October Films, Good Machine, and the once-mighty Miramax. However, since many lesser, mainstream-oriented films also benefited from the scene's prestige, over time the "indie spirit" became more of a label than a true ethic. Some of the major studios created supposedly autonomous subsidiaries, such as Fox Searchlight Pictures, aiming to capture some of the indie spirit under their own roofs.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from The Blair Witch Project
information.contentText: The 3 actors were given lessons in how to handle a camera and were then taken to spend eight days in the forest, deprived of sleep and food, with only a compass and without even knowing where they were. The crew was camouflaged and hidden in the middle of the forest. Everything was done to make the film seem more real. By day, between takes, they were given ideas for improvised lines. At night, the crew frightened them with noises, screams, witchcraft objects, notes meant to sow discord, and everything else that can be seen in the film. They never knew what was going to happen or what they would find, because the documentary was real: it dealt with a subject that may not exist, but it was real.

content_list.content_text: Many filmmakers take a "one for them, one for me" approach, alternating between a film made at the studio's behest and one seasoned with their own idiosyncrasies. With the Hellboy films (2004-2008) sandwiching Pan's Labyrinth (2006), Mexican director Guillermo del Toro (b. 1964) was able to explore a Spanish-language story closer to his heart while also producing more commercial adventures drawn from comic books.

Rodriguez alternated between Spy Kids (2001) and the more experimental Sin City (2005) and Planet Terror (2007). Likewise, Soderbergh moved between unabashedly glossy productions (the Ocean's Eleven trilogy, 2001-2007) and risky ventures bordering on the avant-garde, such as The Girlfriend Experience (2009).

information.contentText: Many interpretations of the film's story are possible. Some say it is nothing more than the boy's hallucinations or a dream, or that the ending simply makes no sense. However, the director's cut, released in 2004, offers clues to one possible interpretation. The film's official website features copies of a few pages from the book "The Philosophy of Time Travel," which suggest that the film takes place in a Tangent Universe, in which Donnie is the "Living Receiver" responsible for returning an "Artifact" to the Primary Universe. And Frank is one of the "Manipulated Dead," who guides the receiver into taking the actions that set off the chain of events. Otherwise, both universes (and everything in them) could be destroyed. According to this interpretation, all the other characters are "manipulated" in ways that lead Donnie to fulfill his duty, making it impossible for him not to.

content_list.content_text: Gus van Sant also flirted with more conventional subjects - Good Will Hunting (1997) - before returning to more abstract material in Gerry (2002) and Elephant (2003). It is also not uncommon for independent directors to take on the lucrative job of script doctoring on Hollywood projects, refreshing mainstream productions with more personal authorial touches: Tarantino worked on Crimson Tide (1995) and Sayles on Apollo 13 (1995).

content_list.title: Little Miss Sunshine: Beyond Appearances
content_list.description:
What sets winners apart from losers? Victories from defeats? What would truly allow a person to avoid failure and be driven to win? And what is the point of this relentless pursuit of winning, in its most normative sense? Just to win? To win for whom? For others? For the world? For oneself? That is how the first feature film by Jonathan Dayton and Valerie Faris premiered at the 2006 Sundance Film Festival, opening on Richard Hoover (Greg Kinnear) giving a talk about his self-help book introducing the nine steps needed to become a winner. Hoover's world is thus divided into two opposing positions: either you win, or you fail. The weight of the family, however, is carried by Sheryl (Toni Collette), wife, mother and the household's main breadwinner. Richard, meanwhile, although he applies the ideas in his book to raising his children, is frustrated at being unable to sell it to any publisher. In the figure of Sheryl's brother, Frank Ginsberg (Steve Carell), a scholar of the writer Proust, lies the tragic theme of the man who failed to kill himself. Forced to stay with his sister's family, Frank is reintroduced to his nephew Dwayne (Paul Dano), who, driven by his desire to become a test pilot, has taken a vow of silence, also as a result of his interest in the writings of Friedrich Nietzsche. But there are still more members of this captivating, relatable family to meet.

Besides those already mentioned, the heart of the story also includes Edwin Hoover (Alan Arkin), Richard's father. Kicked out of a retirement home over problems with heroin, this old man ends up developing his more human side in the bond he nurtures with Olive (Abigail Breslin), the couple's daughter, who sees in her grandfather the coach responsible for keeping alive her aspiring dreams of becoming Little Miss Sunshine. When the family learns that Olive has unexpectedly qualified to compete for the title, they all set off on a trip to Redondo Beach, crammed into a charming – and rusty – yellow Volkswagen bus. Michael Arndt's screenplay then throws the viewer into a far-from-conventional journey. The road trip formula is unquestionably successful when it carries a deep study of the idea of family, both as a whole and in its individuality. On the other hand, there are some questionable aspects to Arndt's work. The most tragic circumstances, which take place both in a motel and in a hospital, open the door to a reckless, almost insensitive, comedic treatment.

Still, even with so many characters and subplots, the center of the story truly mirrors the journey of Olive, the Hoovers' naive and adorable daughter; the absolute soul of a gracefully revitalizing film. Young as she is, Abigail Breslin (b. 1996) wins over the audience playing a little girl who, though prone to insecurity, manages to overcome her fears, which are as powerful to her mind as adult fears are to the minds of grown-ups. The difference is that, while most adults prolong their own ordeals, Olive finds the key to getting past her fears and, on top of that, to getting past the worst nightmares of her loved ones. Even if it takes a few questionable routes, Little Miss Sunshine, a top-tier feel-good movie, is deeply surprising, bringing a spectacular cast, a committed screenplay, an emotional score and proficient direction. In the girl's mission to become Little Miss Sunshine, the family members redeem themselves, not by solving their problems, but by finding peace in the people with whom they will walk through the sea of challenges life brings. Victory, after all, lies not in the absence of defeat, but in the resolve to stand firm in the face of obstacles, which, even when they knock us down, need not necessarily crush hope, which, through thick and thin, will always remain.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the article "Crítica | Pequena Miss Sunshine" (Review | Little Miss Sunshine), by Gabriel Carvalho at Plano Crítico.

content_list.content_text: Throughout his career, the director-actor-screenwriter Orson Welles (1915-1985) clashed with the studios in a struggle for control, seeking a way to complete his vision. The situation is no different in today's Hollywood, and successful directors such as the Coen brothers insist on having the final say over the editing of their work, ensuring that their films stand apart from Hollywood conventions. The challenge for American independent filmmakers is to offer audiences genuine alternatives to the themes and practices of standard Hollywood production.

Indeed, independent films can be box-office hits: Little Miss Sunshine (2006) and Paranormal Activity (2007), a horror film with a microscopic budget, are recent examples. Another is Catfish (2010), which became famous on the back of a controversy over its supposedly documentary nature.

information.contentText: The film premiered at the Sundance Film Festival on January 20, 2006, and its distribution rights were bought by Fox Searchlight Pictures in one of the most expensive deals in the festival's history. It had a limited release in the United States on July 26, followed by a wide release on August 18.

content_list.content_text: Since the turn of the 21st century, the health of American independent cinema has drained away noticeably, but as equipment costs fall, the internet market grows and Hollywood's creativity stagnates, a resurgence of independent production should not be ruled out.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Jonathan Romney, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

movies.title: Pulp Fiction
movies.overview: A burger-loving hit man, his philosophical partner, a drug-addled gangster's moll and a washed-up boxer converge in this sprawling, comedic crime caper. Their adventures unfurl in three stories that ingeniously trip back and forth in time.

movies.title: Sex, Lies, and Videotape
movies.overview: A sexually repressed woman's husband is having an affair with her sister. The arrival of a visitor with a rather unusual fetish changes everything.

movies.title: Fargo
movies.overview: Jerry, a small-town Minnesota car salesman is bursting at the seams with debt... but he's got a plan. He's going to hire two thugs to kidnap his wife in a scheme to collect a hefty ransom from his wealthy father-in-law. It's going to be a snap and nobody's going to get hurt... until people start dying. Enter Police Chief Marge, a coffee-drinking, parka-wearing - and extremely pregnant - investigator who'll stop at nothing to get her man. And if you think her small-time investigative skills will give the crooks a run for their ransom... you betcha!

movies.title: Good Will Hunting
movies.overview: Will Hunting has a genius-level IQ but chooses to work as a janitor at MIT. When he solves a difficult graduate-level math problem, his talents are discovered by Professor Gerald Lambeau, who decides to help the misguided youth reach his potential. When Will is arrested for attacking a police officer, Professor Lambeau makes a deal to get leniency for him if he will get treatment from therapist Sean Maguire.

movies.title: The Blair Witch Project
movies.overview: In October of 1994 three student filmmakers disappeared in the woods near Burkittsville, Maryland, while shooting a documentary. A year later their footage was found.

movies.title: The Royal Tenenbaums
movies.overview: Royal Tenenbaum and his wife Etheline had three children and then they separated. All three children are extraordinary --- all geniuses. Virtually all memory of the brilliance of the young Tenenbaums was subsequently erased by two decades of betrayal, failure, and disaster. Most of this was generally considered to be their father's fault. "The Royal Tenenbaums" is the story of the family's sudden, unexpected reunion one recent winter.

movies.title: Lost in Translation
movies.overview: Two lost souls visiting Tokyo -- the young, neglected wife of a photographer and a washed-up movie star shooting a TV commercial -- find an odd solace and pensive freedom to be real in each other's company, away from their lives in America.

movies.title: El Mariachi
movies.overview: El Mariachi just wants to play his guitar and carry on the family tradition. Unfortunately, the town he tries to find work in has another visitor, a killer who carries his guns in a guitar case. The drug lord and his henchmen mistake el Mariachi for the killer, Azul, and chase him around town trying to kill him and get his guitar case.

movies.title: Clerks
movies.overview: Convenience and video store clerks Dante and Randal are sharp-witted, potty-mouthed and bored out of their minds. So in between needling customers, the counter jockeys play hockey on the roof, visit a funeral home and deal with their love lives.

movies.title: Dead Man
movies.overview: On the run after murdering a man, accountant William Blake encounters a strange North American man named Nobody who prepares him for his journey into the spiritual world.

movies.title: Donnie Darko
movies.overview: After narrowly escaping a bizarre accident, a troubled teenager is plagued by visions of a large bunny rabbit that manipulates him to commit a series of crimes.

movies.title: Happiness
movies.overview: The lives of many individuals connected by the desire for happiness, often from sources usually considered dark or evil.

movies.title: Being John Malkovich
movies.overview: One day at work, unsuccessful puppeteer Craig finds a portal into the head of actor John Malkovich. The portal soon becomes a passion for anybody who enters its mad and controlling world of overtaking another human body.

movies.title: Reservoir Dogs
movies.overview: A botched robbery indicates a police informant, and the pressure mounts in the aftermath at a warehouse. Crime begets violence as the survivors -- veteran Mr. White, newcomer Mr. Orange, psychopathic parolee Mr. Blonde, bickering weasel Mr. Pink and Nice Guy Eddie -- unravel.

movies.title: Sin City
movies.overview: Welcome to Sin City. This town beckons to the tough, the corrupt, the brokenhearted. Some call it dark… Hard-boiled. Then there are those who call it home — Crooked cops, sexy dames, desperate vigilantes. Some are seeking revenge, others lust after redemption, and then there are those hoping for a little of both. A universe of unlikely and reluctant heroes still trying to do the right thing in a city that refuses to care.

movies.title: Little Miss Sunshine
movies.overview: A family loaded with quirky, colorful characters piles into an old van and road trips to California for little Olive to compete in a beauty pageant.

movies.title: Slacker
movies.overview: Austin, Texas, is an Eden for the young and unambitious, from the enthusiastically eccentric to the dangerously apathetic. Here, the nobly lazy can eschew responsibility in favor of nursing their esoteric obsessions. The locals include a backseat philosopher who passionately expounds on his dream theories to a seemingly comatose cabbie, a young woman who tries to hawk Madonna's Pap test to anyone who will listen and a kindly old anarchist looking for recruits.

content_list.description: '90s independent cinema dominates the screens, and animation breaks new ground with Pixar. CGI reaches a new level with The Matrix, and Latin American and European cinemas capture the world's attention. Click here to see a chronological view of the main events in cinema from 1990 to 2009.
